Likewise, gold can be produced from it just as from other metals, unless it is deprived of its heat or its natural operation is not taken away from it. But if the power of a greater natural heat approaches that <term>quicksilver</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss> before it has been formed into its final state—namely into the form of silver—so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of Nature, then gold is formed from it more quickly than silver. And it remains in that state perpetually, as the end toward which Nature tends by its labor.

The <term>quicksilver</term> we have just mentioned is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and moisture. If it is made pure and separated from all superfluity, then no further coarseness can be mixed with it, such that it would be reduced back into some imperfect metal. For Nature does not work backward, nor is it a matter that looks toward any impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But <term>sulfur</term> is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this distinction, let it be observed how <term>quicksilver</term> is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

There is therefore in all metals a true <term>Mercury</term> and a right <term>sulfur</term>, equally in the imperfect as in the perfect metals. They have merely been contaminated and made impure in the imperfect metals, which alone are deprived of perfect maturation. For these same reasons, they can be reduced to gold and silver; that is, so that the impurity with which they had been defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is within them, and the form of gold or silver may be introduced into them. For they have been torn away from Nature because they were removed and dug out from their natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth. Therefore, they can no longer have any operation within themselves as if they were still lying hidden under the earth; nevertheless, as much as is within them, they desire to be perfected.

To this natural property also belongs the Spirit of Truth, who <note>The text continues on the next page regarding the role of the Spirit of Truth in the perfection of metals.</note>

<summary>The author describes the generation of silver and gold from the primary principles of sulfur and mercury, asserting that all base metals contain the potential for perfection if their impurities are removed. He argues that metals removed from the earth cease their natural growth but retain an internal desire for maturation into gold.</summary>
